name: Loess Hills
blurb: Wind-blown silt ridges where remnant prairie, fire and spreading cedar shape the web.

tip.title: Take away fire
tip.text: Fire holds back red cedar and keeps the bluff prairie open. Set Fire to -100% and watch the grasses, then the voles, deer and the predators that depend on them.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.desc: A tall warm-season grass that dominates the remnant prairie on the loess ridges and feeds many grazers and seed eaters.
A shorter bunchgrass that thrives on the dry, steep bluff tops and south-facing slopes of the hills.

nodes.name: Common milkweed
nodes.desc: A prairie wildflower and the host plant for monarch caterpillars; its flowers also feed bees and other pollinators.

nodes.name: Eastern red cedar
nodes.desc: A fire-intolerant evergreen that spreads into prairie where fire is suppressed, shading out grasses; its berries feed birds and mammals.
Its caterpillars feed only on milkweed, so prairie milkweed patches are a key resource for this migratory butterfly.

nodes.name: Brown-belted bumble bee
nodes.desc: A common bumble bee that visits leadplant, milkweed and other prairie flowers for nectar and pollen.
A small grass-eating rodent of dry grassy fields, prey for coyotes, hawks, owls, foxes and snakes.
The common large herbivore of the hills, grazing and browsing prairie plants and supplying carrion for scavengers.

nodes.name: American robin
nodes.desc: A very widely recorded omnivore that eats insects, worms and fruit, and is itself prey for hawks, snakes and raccoons.
A tiny, voracious insectivore that also takes voles and other small animals; eaten by hawks, coyotes and badgers.
A large constrictor of open grassland that eats small mammals such as voles and pocket gophers, plus ground-nesting birds and their eggs.
A burrowing carnivore named among the hills' mammals; it digs out small mammals and also scavenges deer carcasses.
An omnivore of woodland edges that eats fruit such as cedar berries along with birds and other small animals.
A soaring scavenger that cleans up carcasses of deer, coyotes and other animals along the bluffs.
A common raptor of the hills, hunting voles, shrews, snakes and birds; many raptors pass along the Missouri River bluffs.
The most widespread large predator here, taking voles, deer, raccoons and many other animals and also eating cedar berries.
A secretive cat reported to be rebounding in the hills; it hunts rodents, rabbits, deer and raccoons.
Warm-season prairie grasses use the strong summer sun, especially on the dry south-facing slopes.
Rain feeds the prairie plants; the bare, steep loess slopes drain fast and run dry between storms.
Fire keeps trees such as red cedar out of the prairie; with fire suppressed, woodland has crept into the grassland.
Fungi and bacteria break down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to the loess soil.
